extracted.intended_audience: judges, patent lawyers, and law students studying equitable remedies for patent infringement
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and principles governing when and how courts of equity will grant or deny injunctions, order accounts of profits, treat licensees and assignees, and apply defenses (laches, public use, estoppel) in patent-infringement disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Profits estimation for accounting
rubrics_metrics.description: Profits are rightly estimated by finding the difference between cost and sales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In estimating cost, the elements of cost of materials, interest, expense of manufacture and sale, and bad debts, considered by a manufacturer in estimating his profits, are to be taken into account, and no others. Profits due to elements not patented, which entered into the composition of the patented article, may sometimes be allowed, but not always. Extraordinary salaries, being in fact dividends of profits allowed under that name, should not be allowed. Interest on capital stock and 'manufacturers' profits' are not to be allowed. (See §436a; Rubber Company v. Goodyear, 9 Wallace, 788.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Account limited to actual gains and profits
rubrics_metrics.description: An account (under a consent decree) is for 'such gains and profits as have accrued to [defendants] from using the said machines' — i.e., such gains and profits actually accrued to the defendants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A consent to an account under the prayer of the bill binds the defendants only as to the perpetual injunction and to an accounting for actual gains and profits; it does not conclude defendants against exceptions to matters in a master's report that would be illegal or oppressive. Equity should not convert an accounting into a punitive award beyond actual accrued profits; courts should not punish simple torts by awarding damages greater than the profits actually received.

rubrics_metrics.name: Master's report/arbitration bindingness
rubrics_metrics.description: If a reference to a master is in the nature of an arbitration, the award of that officer is binding unless assailed for fraud, misbehavior, or gross mistake of fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a master's report functions like an arbitration award, it will be treated as binding; challenges must be brought on narrow grounds (fraud, misconduct, gross factual mistake). However, courts must ensure the master's instructions and scope conform to the consent decree/prayer of the bill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity not a vehicle for punitive damages for simple torts
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts of equity are not to be converted into instruments for the punishment of simple torts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equitable accounting and injunction remedies should aim at compensation and protection of rights rather than vengeance or punishment. Awards based on conjectural profit rates or to punish wrongdoing (beyond actual injury) are inconsistent with equitable principles (criticized where a master doubled compensation and court added interest as penalty).

rubrics_metrics.name: Injunction should not be dissolved for technical/administrative doubts
rubrics_metrics.description: An injunction should not be dissolved merely on account of doubts as to the validity of the patent which arise from objections to the technical form or signature of the letters, or other acts or omissions of the public officers, and not from any neglect or wrong of the patentee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Doubts that concern mere formalities or clerical acts by Patent Office officials (signature, form, clerical mistakes) are not sufficient to dissolve an injunction already granted; by contrast, doubts going to the merits (originality, usefulness, or the patentee's own error in specification) may justify different treatment. See quoted opinion of Justice Woodbury (Woodworth v. Hall) and Sparkman v. Higgins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delay in prosecution not necessarily fatal to injunction
rubrics_metrics.description: Delay in the steps necessary to acquisition of the patent is not sufficient ground for dissolving an injunction provided such delay was not usual and the application was followed up with reasonable diligence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equitable relief will be refused for unreasonable delay (laches), but mere delay in prosecution, if reasonable and diligently pursued, does not alone require dissolution of an injunction. The court examines the circumstances and whether delay caused prejudice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee's prior commercialization not automatically fatal
rubrics_metrics.description: The patentee having sold the manufactured article is not, by that fact alone, sufficient ground to dissolve an injunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commercialization or sale of the patented article before enforcement does not automatically bar equitable relief; the court considers whether the patentee's conduct amounts to acquiescence, laches, or otherwise undermines exclusive possession required for an injunction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent Office misinformation not binding on patentee for injunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: If third parties, inquiring at the Patent Office, are informed that no patent has been obtained and act upon the information, the patentee is not bound by such action of the Patent Office officials, and a temporary injunction granted him cannot be dissolved on that ground.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public statements by officials that are erroneous do not estop the patentee or automatically dissolve equitable relief; courts will look to patentee's conduct and ultimate rights rather than administrative mistakes (Sparkman v. Higgins).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equitable treatment of licensees and license forfeiture
rubrics_metrics.description: A licensee who has obtained a license upon certain terms will be held to compliance with those terms; equity acts with due regard to substantial rights of both parties, neither permitting the licensee to continue use in disregard of the agreement nor working an unreasonable forfeiture of the license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may refuse an unconditional injunction that would effectively annul a license where the licensee has breached (e.g., Brooks v. Stolley). If a licensee stops paying under an annual-rent contract and continues use, patentee may sue for rent or infringement; when the validity of the patent is contested and the defendant is not estopped, plaintiff must give opportunity to contest validity (plaintiff may be required to pay money into court to await legal determination). Whether a breach effects forfeiture depends on contract terms and circumstances; equity will not cancel contracts except for fraud or mistake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of receipt of royalties on treating prior breaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Acceptance of royalties after an alleged ground of forfeiture may constitute a conclusive election not to treat prior breaches as a ground of forfeiture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Receipt of payments (royalties) by the licensor, after the alleged breach, can be treated as an election to continue the license rather than terminate it (Warwick v. Hooper). Courts will analogize principles from landlord-tenant forfeiture law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on enjoining assignees for assignor's breaches
rubrics_metrics.description: The patentee has no lien on the license to secure unpaid tariffs; unpaid tariffs due by the assignor afford no ground for enjoining the assignees under the license (unless other equitable grounds exist).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assignees who take with notice may still in some circumstances avoid injunctions based solely on assignor's unpaid obligations; fraudulent assignment to evade prior decrees raises issues only once the prior decree is final. See Goodyear v. The Congress Rubber Co.

rubrics_metrics.name: When patentee assigns whole interest, remedy limited to covenant
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the patentee assigns his whole interest in the patent, reserving merely an annual income to be paid by the grantee, he can have no action either at law or in equity under the patent; his only remedy for non-payment of the income is an action upon the covenant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transfer that passes entire legal and equitable title leaves the assignor without standing to sue under the patent; the grantee holds the patent rights and enforcement rests with the grantee. (Hartshorn v. Day.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Public use prior to patent as equitable defense
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a good defence in equity to a bill for a perpetual injunction that, prior to the granting of the patent, the inventor had allowed the invention to go into public use without objection, but it must be clearly established by proof that such public use was with the knowledge and consent of the inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory defenses based on public use or prior public disclosure can be asserted in equity as well as at law; the defendant must prove inventor's knowledge/consent to the public use (Wyeth v. Stone).

rubrics_metrics.name: Laches and acquiescence bar to equitable relief
rubrics_metrics.description: The court will not lend its extraordinary aid to any claimant who has encouraged or acquiesced in an infringement of his right, or who has unreasonably delayed prosecuting for such violation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence that the patentee knew of widespread disregard of the exclusive right and failed to act, or that there has been an unreasonable delay (laches), will lead to dismissal of the bill for injunction. Courts assess the plaintiff's vigilance, means of information, and prejudice to defendants (Lewis v. Chapman).
